title: Stress Related to Individual Life Circumstances and Worry About Global Issues as Distinct but Related Predictors of Psychological Health in Canadian Young Adults.
abstract: Young adults' psychological health has deteriorated in many developed countries over the past decade, including Canada. To further understand this negative trend, this study documented stress related to individual life circumstances (e.g., finances, housing) and worry about global issues (e.g., climate change, world conflicts) and investigated their cross-sectional and prospective associations with psychological health. A sample of 1149 individuals from Canada (M = 24.84, SD = 2.75) completed an online questionnaire in Winter 2025. Of these, 517 participants completed a six-month follow-up. Between 25% and 64% of participants reported being moderately to highly stressed about their life circumstances. Similarly, 32%-43% reported being frequently to constantly worried about global issues. Individual stressors were associated with greater distress (anxiety, depression) and lower well-being at T1, but not at T2, whereas global-issue-related worry was associated with greater distress at T1, and with higher anxiety and lower well-being at T2. Moderation analyses revealed that global-issue-related worry at T1 was positively associated with well-being, but only at high levels of individual stress whereas the negative association between individual stressors and well-being was weaker among participants who reported worrying more frequently about global issues. In addition to revealing an interplay between individual and collective issues, these findings highlight the relevance of global-issue-related worry to young adults' psychological health, with statistically significant associations observed across both concurrent and prospective assessments. Efforts to promote young Canadians' mental health may therefore benefit from considering and addressing both their individual life circumstances and broader societal conditions.
